channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Rail
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] FBI seizes the Chinese state-sponsored platforms that scanned US critical infrastructure and relayed the attacks through hijacked devices
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms run by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY and ties to a Nanjing contractor. QScan performed reconnaissance against US critical infrastructure; QTRouter relayed the resulting intrusions through compromised routers and IoT devices so traffic arrived from ordinary domestic addresses. Both are now inoperable because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware for command and authentication. Named victims are federal, and the described activity runs back to at least 2018. For railroads and transit agencies the relay layer is the transferable point: a rail estate is full of small, internet-connected, unpatched devices — and the source address in your logs never proved anything. - US Department of Justice press release and unsealed court documents — corroborated by TechCrunch and UPI - Seizures announced and confirmed 26 Aug 2026; described activity dates from at least 2018 to 2026

item.title: [Critical] A cyberattack put a rail-served inland port onto manual gate processing
item.description: North Carolina Ports confirmed a cyberattack that disrupted IT systems across the Port of Wilmington, the Port of Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port, the last of which is a rail-served intermodal facility. The incident was detected on 4 August, the authority activated its cybersecurity contingency plan, and recovery began the next morning with operations moved to manual gate processing. The Coast Guard and state officials monitored the response. For railroads the relevance is the interchange: intermodal volumes depend on a terminal operating system that is not yours, and when it goes down your equipment sits while someone else recovers. No attribution or technical detail has been published. - North Carolina Ports statements — reported by BleepingComputer, The Record, CyberScoop and Maritime Executive - Attack detected 4 Aug 2026; recovery began 5 Aug 2026; operations largely restored by 7 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Treasury sanctions an Iranian intelligence-directed hacking network operating inside US critical infrastructure
item.category: Incident — Nation-state targeting of US critical infrastructure
item.description: The US Treasury designated an Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security-directed hacking network on 24 August as part of a wider action covering nearly 60 Iran-linked people, entities and vessels, with a related State Department reward notice. Treasury states the network has breached and exfiltrated data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. Rail is not named, but the tradecraft described — harvesting credentials, vendor footholds and network documentation — is sector-agnostic, and earlier federal reporting has flagged Iranian-affiliated interest in internet-connected control devices used across transportation. Treat this as a targeting signal rather than an incident notification. - US Treasury press release and OFAC designations; State Department Rewards for Justice notice; reported via The Record, Nextgov/FCW and The Hacker News - Designations announced 24 Aug 2026; press analysis 25 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] An attacker crossed a shared private cellular network from one operator’s site into another’s plant
item.category: Incident — Lateral movement across a shared carrier network
item.description: CERT Polska’s follow-up report describes an intrusion that began at a wind farm and ended at an unrelated combined heat and power plant, where a turbine was taken out of service. The bridge was a private APN both organisations bought from the same carrier. A private APN is an addressing and billing construct, not a security boundary. Railroads and transit agencies should read this closely because cellular is the default connectivity for anything trackside: crossing monitors, signal-house telemetry, defect detectors, remote switch heaters, station equipment and positive train control backhaul. If those devices sit on a shared APN and can address one another, the isolation you assumed may not exist. - CERT Polska incident follow-up report — via Help Net Security, BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and The Hacker News - Incident 29 Dec 2025; CERT Polska disclosure 8 Aug 2026; press analysis 11 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA’s red team took a domain undetected — the tooling was fine, the monitoring was not
item.category: Threat intel — Federal red-team assessment findings
item.description: CISA advisory AA26-237A publishes paired red-team results from two critical-infrastructure organisations assessed with comparable tradecraft. One detected and responded; the other never noticed a domain compromise. The advisory is direct that the difference was not product spend — both had capable tooling, but only one reviewed the output, correlated identity events and had practised the response. Transit agencies and railroads recognise the pattern because dispatch, maintenance, fare collection and corporate systems so often share one Active Directory, and because operational networks are frequently left outside monitoring on the grounds that the alerts would be too noisy to action. - CISA advisory AA26-237A — corroborated by CyberScoop and The Hacker News - Published 25 Aug 2026; verified against the CISA advisory 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Five agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers on exposed networks
item.category: Threat intel — Joint federal advisory on ICS protocol tooling
item.description: Joint advisory AA26-231A from NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA describes actors using AI assistance to build custom tooling from a well-documented open-source S7 library, querying internet-exposed Siemens S7 controllers in traffic that resembles legitimate monitoring. The agencies assess the activity as reconnaissance and pre-positioning. Rail is not a named sector, but SIMATIC controllers are widespread in station and depot systems, platform screen doors, traction power auxiliaries, washplants and maintenance facilities. The change that matters is that protocol expertise no longer gates who can interrogate a controller — so an exposed S7 in a depot is being read by a larger population than it was a year ago. - NSA / CISA / FBI / DOE / EPA joint advisory AA26-231A, building on AA26-097A — via CISA, BleepingComputer and Industrial Cyber - AA26-231A published 19 Aug 2026; builds on AA26-097A from April 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in a quarter, and none of them needed the control system touched
item.category: Threat intel — Quarterly industrial ransomware analysis
item.description: Dragos counted 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up around 12 percent on the first, and drew out the point that attackers do not need control-system access to disrupt operations. The rail translation is straightforward: nobody needs to reach a signalling system to degrade a railroad. Encrypting crew calling, work order and maintenance management, car and consist tracking, fare collection or customer information produces delays, cancellations and manual working on its own. Those systems rarely receive the segmentation, backup validation or restoration testing applied to safety-critical signalling. - Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis, Q2 2026 — via Dragos and Help Net Security - Report covers Q2 2026; published and reported 11 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue from a patching recommendation to confirmed exploitation in the wild. It is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, needing no authentication, and reachable when the appliance is configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre reported indications of exploitation from around 17 August after a public proof of concept. In rail and transit organisations NetScaler frequently fronts the remote access used by dispatch support staff, maintenance contractors and signalling suppliers. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition of 26 Aug 2026 and Citrix security bulletin — corroborated by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and watchTowr Labs analysis - Vendor patches released August 2026; exploitation indications from 17 Aug; added to KEV 26 Aug 2026; federal deadline 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] A Git server exploit in KEV — and it is where signalling and station configuration often lives
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, engineering toolchain
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-60004 to the KEV catalogue on 25 August after reports of active exploitation. Rated CVSS 9.8, the flaw lets anyone with ordinary repository write access plant an executable Git hook and run shell commands as the Gitea service account. Gitea 1.27.1 fixed it on 27 July, so exploitation followed within a month. Self-hosted Gitea turns up in rail engineering groups because it is easy to stand up for station and depot PLC projects, SCADA screens, passenger information configuration and integration scripts. A modest contractor account then becomes code execution on the machine holding operational configuration. Federal remediation was due 28 August. - CISA KEV catalogue addition — corroborated by Help Net Security, SecurityWeek and The Hacker News - Gitea 1.27.1 released 27 Jul 2026; added to KEV 25 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] August ICS Patch Tuesday: Ruggedcom and Desigo alongside a maximum-severity IoT2050 flaw
item.category: Advisory — August ICS Patch Tuesday, Siemens estate
item.description: Siemens published ten advisories in its August set, alongside Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact, with CISA issuing companion ICS advisories the same week. The headline item is a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices allowing unauthenticated remote code execution with elevated privileges. Rail estates are exposed to more of this batch than most sectors, because Siemens equipment spans the environment: Ruggedcom networking in signal houses and substations, Desigo building automation at stations and depots, Siveillance video management, and SIMATIC controllers in auxiliary and depot systems. Review the whole set rather than only the maximum-severity entry. - Siemens ProductCERT August 2026 advisories and the CISA ICS advisory batch — reported by SecurityWeek - Published 12 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] No login required and no patch coming — the Ebyte gateway advisory is a replacement decision
item.category: Advisory — Serial-to-Ethernet gateway, no vendor patch
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-237-06 covers the Ebyte NE2-D11 serial-to-Ethernet gateway, whose web management interface does not consistently enforce authentication before granting administrative functionality. An unauthenticated remote attacker can read configuration, change settings, hijack sessions or disrupt operation. CISA notes the vendor acknowledged the reports, said a patch was in development, then stopped responding. Low-cost serial converters of this class are common across rail estates, sitting behind older equipment at crossings, in signal houses, at fuelling points and in depot test rigs — installed because something legacy needed a network connection, and rarely recorded anywhere afterwards. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-237-06, reported by researcher Jithin Nambiar — via CISA - Published 25 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026 — no vendor patch announced

item.title: [High] An exploited Windows IKE flaw — pre-authentication SYSTEM on the box terminating your site-to-site VPN
item.category: Advisory — Exploited Windows IKE flaw in KEV
item.description: CISA added four exploited vulnerabilities to KEV on 18 August, including a Windows Internet Key Exchange flaw permitting pre-authentication code execution as SYSTEM. Microsoft shipped the fix in April, so the gap is deployment rather than availability. Placement makes it relevant to a railroad: IKE runs on the hosts terminating site-to-site tunnels, and those tunnels are how a control centre reaches a remote territory, how a depot reaches head office, and how a signalling or rolling-stock supplier reaches diagnostic equipment. Pre-authentication compromise of that endpoint puts an attacker at the junction of both networks. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue and Microsoft security updates — via CISA and The Hacker News - Added to CISA KEV 18 Aug 2026; vendor patch issued April 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] A hard-coded key in Johnson Controls Airwall — the product many sites use to protect everything else
item.category: Advisory — Hard-coded key in a segmentation product
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-03 republishes a Johnson Controls advisory covering a hard-coded cryptographic key in Airwall, alongside an arbitrary file read issue. Airwall is a micro-segmentation and secure-remote-access product, deployed to isolate operational networks and broker vendor access. A weakness in a compensating control deserves more attention than the same weakness in an ordinary application, because the architecture assumes the device holds. In rail and transit environments Airwall and comparable products frequently sit between corporate IT and station, depot or building systems, which makes this more than a routine patch item. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-225-03, republishing the Johnson Controls advisory — via CISA - Published 13 Aug 2026 in CISA’s mid-August advisory batch; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] The TSA rail directive runs to 15 January 2027 while the surface cyber rule remains proposed
item.category: Policy — TSA rail security directive and pending rulemaking
item.description: Security Directive 1580-21-01E, the current TSA cybersecurity directive for designated freight and passenger railroads, is effective from 16 January 2026 through 15 January 2027. Its performance-based requirements — network segmentation between IT and OT, access control, continuous monitoring and timely patching, together with a cybersecurity implementation plan and assessment programme — remain the operative obligation. The broader “Enhancing Surface Cyber Risk Management” rulemaking, published for comment in November 2024 and closed to comment in February 2025, would convert the directives into permanent regulation including 24-hour incident reporting to CISA, but no final rule has been issued. - TSA Security Directive 1580-21-01E and the “Enhancing Surface Cyber Risk Management” notice of proposed rulemaking — via TSA and the Federal Register - SD 1580-21-01E effective 16 Jan 2026 through 15 Jan 2027; NPRM published 7 Nov 2024, comments closed 5 Feb 2025; no final rule as of 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] From 11 September 2026 exploited vulnerabilities in digital products must be reported within 24 hours
item.category: Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligation
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations begin on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must notify an actively exploited vulnerability in their product, or a severe incident affecting its security, within 24 hours of becoming aware, with fuller reporting to follow. Railways sit on both sides of this. Operators buying rolling stock, signalling and station systems from European suppliers gain a defined notification obligation to write into contracts; operators or subsidiaries that themselves place connected products on the EU market acquire the obligation directly. - EU Regulation 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act) and European Commission implementation guidance - Regulation entered into force 10 Dec 2024; reporting obligations apply from 11 Sep 2026; full application 11 Dec 2027; status verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] The NSA is putting an ISA/IEC 62443 certificate in front of the controllers it buys
item.description: ISASecure announced a partnership with the National Security Agency to develop a High Criticality Component Security Assurance certification scheme, derived from its Component Security Assurance programme and grounded in ISA/IEC 62443-4-2. Once accepted, the NSA intends to use it when adding OT components to the National Security Systems product compliant list. Rail is not the target market, but the mechanism is what matters: a large buyer making certification a purchase condition changes what vendors build, and the language migrates into other specifications. For an agency writing a station systems or depot automation tender, that is a citable standard rather than an invented requirement. - ISA / ISASecure press release — corroborated by Automation World and ISSSource - Announced 20 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026
